title: Retirement and Death of a Partner
description: Class 12 Accountancy: retirement and death of a partner — gaining ratio, treatment of goodwill, revaluation and reserves, settlement of the retiring partner's dues, and the deceased partner's executor's account.

topics.title: Gaining Ratio and Treatment of Goodwill
topics.concept:
When a partner retires (or dies), the continuing partners take over his share of profits, so they gain. The reverse of admission applies. The gaining ratio = New Ratio − Old Ratio — the ratio in which the remaining partners acquire the outgoing partner's share, and the ratio in which they bear the goodwill compensation.

  • If the remaining partners continue in their old mutual ratio, the gaining ratio = their old ratio.
  • If a new ratio is specified, deduct old from new for each.

Worked example. A, B and C share 3:2:1. B retires; A and C continue equally (1:1). A's gain = 1/2 − 3/6 = 0; C's gain = 1/2 − 1/6 = 2/6. Hmm — better to take a clean case: A, B, C share 4:3:2 and B retires, A and C continuing in 4:2 (= 2:1). Old A 4/9, new A 2/3 = 6/9 → gain 2/9; old C 2/9, new C 1/3 = 3/9 → gain 1/9. Gaining ratio 2:1.

Goodwill on retirement. The retiring partner is entitled to his share of the firm's goodwill, which the gaining partners pay. Following AS-26, no goodwill account is raised; instead an adjustment entry is passed:

Gaining Partners' Capital A/cs  Dr (in gaining ratio)
   To Retiring Partner's Capital A/c

The amount = firm's goodwill × the retiring partner's share. For example, if goodwill is Rs 90,000 and the retiring partner's share was 1/3, his share of goodwill = Rs 30,000, debited to the gaining partners in their gaining ratio and credited to him. So retirement mirrors admission: there the newcomer pays; here the gainers pay the leaver.

examples.problem: Example 1: Write the formula for gaining ratio.
examples.solution:
New minus old.

  • Gaining ratio = New share − Old share.
examples.answer: Gaining ratio = New share − Old share.

examples.problem: Example 2: Goodwill is Rs 60,000; the retiring partner's share was 1/4. What is his share of goodwill?
examples.answer: Rs 15,000 (paid by the gaining partners in the gaining ratio).

examples.problem: Example 3: Who bears the retiring partner's share of goodwill?
examples.solution:
The gainers.

  • The continuing (gaining) partners, in their gaining ratio.
examples.answer: The continuing (gaining) partners, in their gaining ratio.

recap:
• On retirement, continuing partners gain; gaining ratio = New − Old.
  • Goodwill entry: Gaining Partners' Capital Dr (gaining ratio) / To Retiring Partner's Capital = goodwill × his share (no goodwill account raised, AS-26).
  • Retirement mirrors admission — here the gainers pay the leaver.

quiz.explanation: Gaining ratio = New share − Old share.

quiz.q: On retirement, the retiring partner's share of goodwill is borne by the:
options: Gaining partners in the gaining ratio
quiz.explanation: The continuing partners pay it in their gaining ratio.

topics.title: Revaluation, Reserves and the Retiring Partner's Dues
topics.concept:
As with any reconstitution, on retirement the firm revalues assets and liabilities and distributes accumulated reserves — but now all partners (including the retiring one) share, because these belong to the old ratio that included him.

  • Revaluation Account — net profit/loss transferred to all partners (including the retiring partner) in the old ratio.
  • Reserves & accumulated profits/losses — distributed to all partners in the old ratio.

After these, the retiring partner's total dues are settled. His capital account is credited with: his capital balance, his share of goodwill (from the gainers), his share of the revaluation profit and reserves, his share of any current profit up to the date of retirement, and salary/interest due; and debited with drawings, interest on drawings and his share of any losses. The resulting balance is the amount payable to him.

This amount may be settled in three ways: (i) paid in full in cash; (ii) transferred to his loan account to be paid in instalments with interest (often 6% p.a. under the Act if not agreed); or (iii) partly cash, partly loan. If paid by loan, his Loan Account carries the balance, and interest is added each year until repaid. For example, if his dues are Rs 1,20,000 and Rs 40,000 is paid in cash, the remaining Rs 80,000 is transferred to his loan account. With the dues computed and the mode of payment decided, the retirement is complete and the continuing partners carry on with adjusted capitals.

examples.problem: Example 1: On retirement, in which ratio is the revaluation profit shared?
examples.solution:
All partners, old ratio.

  • Among all partners (including the retiring one) in the old ratio.
examples.answer: Among all partners (including the retiring partner) in the old ratio.

examples.problem: Example 2: List three items credited to the retiring partner's capital account.
examples.solution:
What he is owed.

  • His capital balance, share of goodwill, and share of revaluation profit/reserves.
examples.answer: His capital balance, share of goodwill, and share of revaluation profit and reserves (also salary/interest due, share of current profit).

examples.problem: Example 3: Dues Rs 1,00,000; Rs 30,000 paid in cash. How is the balance treated?
examples.solution:
To loan account.

  • Remaining 70,000 transferred to his loan account (with interest).
examples.answer: Rs 70,000 transferred to the retiring partner's loan account, carrying interest until repaid.

recap:
• On retirement, revaluation profit/loss and reserves go to all partners (incl. retiring) in the old ratio.
  • Retiring partner's dues = capital + goodwill share + revaluation/reserve share + current profit + salary/interest − drawings/losses.
  • Settlement: full cash, transfer to loan account (interest, 6% p.a. if not agreed), or part-cash part-loan.

quiz.q: On retirement, accumulated reserves are distributed to:
options: All partners in the old ratio
quiz.explanation: All partners (including the retiring one) share, in the old ratio.

quiz.q: If the retiring partner's dues are not paid at once, they are transferred to his:
quiz.explanation: Unpaid dues go to his loan account, carrying interest.

topics.title: Death of a Partner and the Executor's Account
topics.concept:
The death of a partner is treated almost exactly like retirement — the main difference is timing (death can occur on any date during the year, not just at year-end) and that the amount due is paid to the deceased partner's executor (legal representative) rather than to the partner himself.

The deceased partner's capital account is credited with the same items as a retiring partner — capital balance, share of goodwill (paid by gainers), share of revaluation profit and reserves — plus two items computed up to the date of death:

  • Share of profit up to the date of death — since accounts are not closed mid-year, his profit share is estimated either on a time basis (last year's profit × months elapsed ÷ 12 × his share) or on a sales basis (profit estimated from sales to date).
  • Interest on capital and any salary due up to the date of death.

The total is transferred to the Executor's Account, which replaces the partner. The executor is then paid — in full or by instalments with interest (6% p.a. if not agreed), exactly like a retiring partner's loan.

For example, if a partner dies three months into the year, his estimated profit share on a time basis = last year's profit × 3/12 × his share. Suppose last year's profit was Rs 1,20,000 and his share 1/4: estimated profit = 1,20,000 × 3/12 × 1/4 = Rs 7,500, credited to his account and ultimately to the executor. With the executor settled, the firm continues with the surviving partners — completing the reconstitution events before the bigger step of dissolution.

examples.problem: Example 1: To whom is the amount due paid on the death of a partner?
examples.solution:
His estate.

  • To the deceased partner's executor (legal representative).
examples.answer: To the deceased partner's executor (legal representative).

examples.problem: Example 2: A partner (share 1/5) dies 4 months into the year. Last year's profit was Rs 90,000. Estimate his profit share on a time basis.
Example 3: Name the two methods of estimating a deceased partner's share of current profit.
examples.solution:
Time or sales.

  • Time basis and sales (turnover) basis.
examples.answer: The time basis and the sales (turnover) basis.

recap:
• Death is treated like retirement, but the amount goes to the executor and is computed to the date of death.
  • Extra items: share of profit to date of death (time basis or sales basis) + interest/salary due.
  • Total → Executor's Account, paid in full or by instalments with interest (6% p.a. if not agreed).

quiz.q: On death, the amount due is transferred to the:
quiz.explanation: It is transferred to the deceased partner's executor's account.

quiz.q: A deceased partner's share of current profit may be estimated on a time basis or a ____ basis.
quiz.explanation: Either a time basis or a sales (turnover) basis is used.

questions.q: When a partner retires, the continuing partners:
questions.explanation: They take over his share, so they gain.

questions.explanation: The gainers pay it in their gaining ratio.

questions.explanation: AS-26 bars self-generated goodwill.

questions.q: Revaluation profit on retirement is shared by:

questions.q: Accumulated reserves on retirement go to:
options: All partners in the old ratio
questions.explanation: All partners in the old ratio.

questions.q: Unpaid dues of a retiring partner are transferred to his:
questions.explanation: Unpaid dues go to his loan account, carrying interest.

questions.q: If not otherwise agreed, interest on a retiring partner's loan under the Act is:
questions.explanation: 6% p.a. applies if not agreed.

questions.q: On death, the amount due is paid to the:
questions.explanation: It is paid to the deceased partner's executor.

questions.q: On death, the amount due is transferred to the:
questions.explanation: It is transferred to the executor's account.

questions.q: A deceased partner's profit to the date of death may be estimated on a time basis or a ____ basis.
questions.explanation: Time basis or sales (turnover) basis.

questions.q: Partner (share 1/5) dies 4 months in; last year's profit Rs 90,000. Time-basis profit =
Death of a partner is treated most like:
questions.explanation: Death is treated like retirement, paid to the executor.

questions.q: Which is credited to a retiring/deceased partner's capital account?
questions.explanation: His share of goodwill is credited (drawings/losses are debited).

questions.q: A, B, C share 4:3:2. B retires; A and C continue in 4:2. The gaining ratio of A and C is:
Goodwill of the firm is Rs 1,08,000; the retiring partner B's share was 1/3. A and C (gaining 2:1) are debited:
Why do ALL partners (including the retiring one) share the revaluation profit, unlike a new partner who does not?
options: The gain arose under the old arrangement that still included the retiring partner
questions.explanation: Revaluation reflects values during the period the retiring partner was a member, so he shares it in the old ratio.

questions.q: B's dues are Rs 2,00,000, paid Rs 50,000 now and the rest in 3 equal annual instalments with 10% interest. The first instalment (principal) is:
questions.explanation: Balance 1,50,000 in 3 equal principal instalments = 50,000 each (plus interest on the outstanding balance).

questions.q: A partner with a 1/4 share dies on 30 June (year ends 31 March). Sales to 30 June were Rs 6,00,000; last year sales Rs 24,00,000 gave a profit of Rs 4,00,000. His profit share on the sales basis is:
On the death of a partner, his share of goodwill is adjusted by:
options: Debiting the gaining partners and crediting the deceased partner's capital
questions.explanation: As in retirement, the gainers bear it via a capital-to-capital adjustment (no goodwill account).

questions.q: If the continuing partners decide to continue in their OLD mutual ratio after a retirement, the gaining ratio equals:
questions.explanation: With no change in their mutual proportions, they gain in the same ratio they already shared.

questions.q: An accumulated loss (debit P&L balance) at retirement is:
options: Debited to all partners in the old ratio
Borne by the retiring partner alone
questions.explanation: Like reserves, an accumulated loss belongs to all partners in the old ratio — here debited.

questions.q: The Executor's Account is essentially the deceased partner's:
options: Loan/payable account that the firm settles over time
questions.explanation: It carries the amount owed to the estate, paid in full or by instalments with interest.

questions.q: Total goodwill of a firm is Rs 1,50,000 and a partner with a 2/5 share retires. The maximum his capital can be credited for goodwill is:
questions.explanation: His share of goodwill = 1,50,000 × 2/5 = 60,000.
